title: Pixi JS Doom style screen wipe (is it possible?), on screen or for individual events?

posts.author: cronenbuilder
posts.body:
Hi all, I'm back with another weird question. I want to ask the community how they would go about leveraging the pixi js graphics system which rpg maker relies on in order to produce a "DooM Style Melting Screen Wipe" on individual event/NPC sprites to simulate the character melting to death/crumbling, etc.
I've been messing around a lot with pixi js lately, mostly just making edits to existing parameters on screen effects but realistically  I have absolutely no idea what I am doing outside of the simplest tinkering.
Carmack's code for the screen wipe is available on git for what I assume is legitimate viewing for whatever that is worth, though it is obviously in a different programming language.

Click to expand...
This wipe effect sounds like a post-process shader, so you could assign a custom
PIXI Filter
to sprites whose character has been marked for wipeout. For a time-dependent shader like a wipe effect, you'd basically just need to give your shader a "time" uniform, then update the value of that uniform on the filter each frame.
MZ creates HTML games that use WebGL, a.k.a. OpenGL ES (Embedded Systems), for rendering. So the final vertex and/or fragment shader code for the wipe effect would have to be in that language.
I don't know if there already exists an MZ plugin for custom time-dependent filters. I suspect the hard part here would be finding/devising suitable shader code.
It could be possible to achieve a similar effect on the CPU, using the
Canvas API
to perform image data edits on a cloned texture (basically
blt
the bitmap every frame). However, that would be much less resource efficient and you'd still need an appropriate algorithm to inform the edits.

posts.author: caethyril
posts.body:
I just realised that for a custom filter a more useful link would probably be the docs for the base class,
PIXI.Filter
. A custom filter can be created like this:
JavaScript:
const VERT = "custom vertex shader code goes here";    // or null for default
const FRAG = "custom fragment shader code goes here";  // or null for default
const UNIFORMS = { time: 0 };  // any custom uniforms referenced in shader code
const f = new PIXI.Filter(VERT, FRAG, UNIFORMS);
PIXI uses some pre-defined structure, so a generic WebGL shader may need editing if it's not already written for use with PIXI.
ColorFilter
defined in rmmz_core.js inherits from
PIXI.Filter
and may be helpful as a reference~
Good luck!

posts.author: caethyril
posts.body:
@utunnels
- not sure what you have in mind, but I was thinking that a snapshot (
SceneManager.snap()
) of the pre-transition scene could have its texture assigned as a uniform to the fragment shader: the shader would then pull color values from the appropriate texture, based on time (and maybe an initial random seed).
I haven't tried writing a shader with a custom texture uniform before, but I looked it up and, based on the fragment shader of the built-in
DisplacementFilter
, that aspect looks fairly simple:
pixijs/src/filters/defaults/displacement/displacement.frag at dev · pixijs/pixijs
The HTML5 Creation Engine: Create beautiful digital content with the fastest, most flexible 2D WebGL renderer. - pixijs/pixijs
github.com
Perhaps it'd be simpler to just show the snapshot as an overlay sprite with a custom "melting" shader.

That plugin you provided is amazing. It is absolutely cool! Here is a brief overview of my experience with it. Upon loading the plugin it works as expected melting the screen into a transition. The screen melts to a black screen, with the enemy visible, any pixi js filters applied are still animating over the enemy which is cool, however the black screen is interesting indicating that the "Scene" was wiped as well.
However, upon using the wipe function on some screens the "Scene" is retained into the battle screen. IE you can still see the background including any events, which is funny because in this instance the enemy is appearing in the battle screen but also still visible as part of the background. I wonder what could cause this discrepancy in scene visualization.
I am willing to work around it because the effect is just amazing, but a fix would be worthwhile.
Additionally can this transition be used for regular scene moving from one map to another transitions?
I can not recommend this effect enough!!!

The trick is you take a screenshot in the previous scene, and use the image to make the effect.
However there's a default fadeout/fadein during map transition. There's also a loading black screen (in MV maybe also MZ?), I haven't checked all scenes but I guess they are a bit different.
